newsitem.title: USA: China wants large ag export subsidy base--US aide.
newsitem.headline: China wants large ag export subsidy base--US aide.

text.p: China wants to maintain its ability to subsidize a large volume of agricultural exports after it joins the World Trade Organization, despite not using export subsidies since 1990, a U.S. official said Thursday.

In the ongoing negotiations on China's bid to join the WTO, "China continues to request a large export subsidy base for... corn, rice, oilseed, oilseed meal, vegetable oil, sugar and tea," said Patricia Sheikh, assistant deputy administrator for trade policy in USDA's Foreign Agricultural Service.
The U.S. opposes that request and is working "vigorously to prevent (it) from actually happening," she said.
In a speech to U.S. sweetener users and cane refiners, Sheikh said China also wants to maintain state trading control over imports of wheat, corn, rice, vegetable oil, sugar, tobacco and cotton.
However, it has agreed to a framework for discussing increased market access for those goods through tariff-rate quotas, Sheikh said.

Under the framework, part of the quotas would be imported by China's state trading enterprises and the rest by "other entities," Sheikh said. Both the state firms and the other buyers could also import in excess of the quota, but that trade would be subject to much higher import duties, she said.
The U.S.'s goal is for China to liberalize its import regime so that imports occur as a result of market dynamics and not "just (as) a function of government decisions," she said.
So far, China has not specified what other domestic buyers might be eligible to participate in the proposed tariff-rate quota trade, Sheikh said.

In another farm trade area, China has made some marginal reductions in some of its prohibitively high import tariffs, Sheikh said. But "it has yet to engage in serious tariff reduction negotiations," she said.
The U.S. also wants China to eliminate "unjustified" plant health and food safety regulations that block imports of U.S. wheat, sugar, plums and tobacco, Sheikh said.
